clips.text: One trip. Every bag. Even the eggs. How did I get it all inside without dropping a thing?
Last Saturday, my sister made four trips from the car. I said I could do it in one. She asked if the eggs had agreed. She had a plan. I had a contest.
Heavy bags on both arms. The bread went on my head.
Three cans swung left. The oranges rolled right. I caught the oranges. The cans did not catch me. By round two, the handles felt like piano wire.
I tried the door with one foot, both hands full.
The door opened. The carton of eggs opened too. My sister said, maybe leave the eggs in the carton. The next morning, an egg rolled out of my shoe.
So I weighed every bag. Cans close. Soft things up top. A spare tote cushioned the handles. My fingers survived. Guessing the bag’s limit helped less.
At last, everything crossed the kitchen in one trip.
Then our neighbor reached the apartment buzzer, both hands full. She had cans, paper bags, and a watermelon. She needed the door. I needed a real test.
I took every grocery bag in one load. Then I pressed the buzzer with my elbow. The door clicked. She carried everything inside.
I carried ours inside in one trip. My sister checked the trunk. It looked empty until she lifted the blanket.
One potato sat alone. I went back for it.
